utterances.text: This is a document that has two documents with it and it is slightly out the sequence in terms of time-frame, but the issue of the dates and the subject matter will be clear. First of all, this is a document dated the 5th of April, 1993, signed by the president of Croatia, Dr. Tudjman. And you can see it is on posting active officer to reserve officer of the Republic of Croatia armed forces. General Cermak was being appointed to the administrative service. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, just to clarify --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- when I said I was not familiar with the background of General Cermak, it was with the -- his activities immediately prior to him being appointed commander of the Knin garrison on the 5th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a look at these things first which can set the background. Page 2 of this document has another document attached to it concerning the 10th of October, 1992, and it's the decision of the president, appointing General Cermak as assistant minister of defence for the state immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may these documents be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D1007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1007 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document, 2D07-0113.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this takes the story up further, Mr. Theunens. And it's the appointment of Mr. Cermak as minister of industry, ship building, and energy by the president, on the 3rd of April, 1993. And we'll get it on the screen soon. There you are. You can see that as part of the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1008, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1008 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Next document is 2D07-0115.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 20th of May, 1993. It's a decision of that date, relieving Mr. Cermak of his duty as minister of industry, ship building, and energy, in the previous appointment that we had seen. And again, issued by the president of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this document may be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1009, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1009 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. 2D07-0117 is the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is dated the 20th of May, 1993, so is following the next -- the previous document. And it's a decision of the president to appoint him as minister of the economy. Were you aware of these appointments, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the formal appointments but have I a recollection that Mr. Cermak was a member of the government during -- at least in 1993. But I didn't have any documents nor the specific documents indicating when he was appointed and to which particular position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1010, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1010 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document is 2D07-0119, and it's the last in this sequence and it follows on from the previous appointment. It's dated the 12th of October, 1993, a decision by the president of Croatia relieving Mr. Cermak of his duty as minister of economy based on his personal request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, did you realize that Mr. Cermak finished his duties as a minister from that date in 1993?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became aware of that, but that was after the filing of the report and also after the filing of the addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1011, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1011 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, D31 is a document that has already been produced into evidence into the proceedings, Mr. Theunens, and it's the appointment of Mr. Cermak as the commander of the Knin garrison and Major Gojevic as the Deputy Commander of the Knin garrison. Did you appreciate that between the period of 1993 until this appointment that Mr. Cermak had held no other public duties or office?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my recollection, I -- yeah, that is correct, and I believe Mr. Cermak was mainly active in private business, as a businessman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's right. And you have correctly referred to him in your report as Colonel in reserve, which we have seen from the earlier appointments, which is what a Colonel General in reserve which we have seen from the earlier appointments. In taking up the task of being a garrison commander without any previous experience in the role, or knowledge of the role, would you agree, would make it difficult to establish an effective garrison in Knin from the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, Your Honours. I mean there are several factors that play a role. The previous commander or acting commander, Gojevic, is appointed as deputy to General Cermak so he could assist with certain matters. As I mentioned, I'm not familiar with the kind of activities or training General Cermak received immediately to -- prior to taking up the position of the Knin garrison. On the other hand, I agree with you that the situation in Knin was quite complex, and that is also visible from the documents I have reviewed, and that it was also a garrison which had not been located in that area prior to the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Such documents as there are and that exist within the OTP database and that have been given to me, we have been through those documents yesterday, you recollect, to show what Major Gojevic did and what his tasks were. Do you recollect that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to this position, you mentioned training. Is that something as a military officer you would deem necessary for a position of this nature?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of garrison commander would require specific training, i.e., I would think a familiarization with the zone of responsibility, or, i.e., the zone covered by the garrison, familiarization with the units, more specifically the commanders of these units that are located in the garrison, and that would take most of time, and on the other hand, also familiarization with the regulations that apply to a garrison commander, as well as all the other aspects that are part of the duty of a garrison commander in a specific area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That deals with training. Also, would you agree, there are resources that are needed to accomplish the tasks of a garrison commander, and I have in mind those matters referred to by the garrison commander of Split whose letter we looked at yesterday?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. And I think it is important in that context to make a distinction between what I would call the proper resources whereby for each unit there is what is called an establishment strength and the establishment strength of the Knin garrison was very small. I believe it was nine, but I'm -- we can check the documents; whereas, for the Split garrison, it was bigger. Obviously depends on the area covered by the garrison. On the other hand, resources also includes units which the garrison commander could use in order to implement his mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of General Forand's view - we have no need to look at the document; it's Exhibit D150 for the Court's benefit - of General Cermak's authority being limited in certain areas, in relation to his role? Were you aware of General Forand's view, in relation to that, as expressed on the 26th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not. And I don't think I have used D150 in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, you haven't.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's been in evidence before the Court, and it's a matter that I'm directing Their Honours's attention to but asking if you were aware of that, and you have given me your answer. Thank you very much. Let us now look at the tasks and job that Mr. Cermak was doing in Knin. I believe you've already referred us to P1144, Exhibit P1144, where, at page 4 in the English transcript of a meeting between the president and Mr. Cermak, there is a discussion about Mr. Cermak being in Knin. You already referred to that earlier in your evidence, and you referred to this transcript. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the one where the president says, Keeping order. Mr. Cermak says, Keeping order, preventing disorder, mine clearance. I took a team with me and we cleared 7.000 buildings and that whole area, et cetera. You referred to that transcript. Were you also aware of a discussion by President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could have D296, transcript for the 7th of August, 1995, and turn to page 20 of the English; page 41 of the Croatian language version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is a discussion of many pages about other matters but during that discussion the issue of what is happening in Knin at that time of the 7th of August, is discussed, and you can see there. These Canadians in Knin, they're all right now, Mr. Zuzul says. Mr. Sanadar makes a reply. Mr. Zuzul says, No, there was. There was the Canadians. The Americans received an official request to assist the Canadians in pulling out of Knin. And the president says, and another thing, tell them I appointed as commander of the Knin garrison, Colonel General Cermak, a former minister, a serious man, to solve those matters. Were you aware of this transcript?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no specific recollection. I am sure I haven't used it and I don't think I saw it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have not used in your report; you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. So there's a small correction to the transcript. I am sure I have not used it. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We seem to have lost my transcript down here at the moment, but -- we've got a power failure. The importance of this issue goes to matters that you have raised in your report and in your evidence frequently concerning Mr. Cermak and the orders to the military police and the Knin police as to being the foundation of your proposition concerning the senior military as well as civilian authority in the area.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But I would also like to mention that the orders Mr. Cermak or General Cermak gives to civilian and the military police are an important component. But there's also the other orders and instructions he issues during the time-period he is the commander of the Knin garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we look at those orders now while we are here, and ... Because there is a point to be made about these orders, and you have mentioned them several times as being important, in relation to your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we go to P512 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the first order to the military police and Knin police, and it is dated the 8th of August, 1995, and the significance is, Mr. Theunens, that it concerns UNCRO. Do you appreciate that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But from the point of view of -- of my task to identify the role of General Cermak as the commander of the Knin garrison, it is also important to take into account that he can -- he -- by this document or this document indicates that he has the authority to issue an order to the military police without specifying which specific unit we are talking about, and the Knin police station, which, in my view, is the civilian police in Knin. We know from documents by General Lausic that there is already a Knin -- excuse me, a military police presence in Knin prior to the 8th of August, but I have not been able to establish over which component or which part of this military police presence in Knin General Cermak has the authority to issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we look at a number of those propositions there in your answer? First of all, the fact that he issues this order doesn't necessarily mean to say that he has the authority to issue it. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we only consider this document, I agree with you. And will see you in my report I have included several of such orders, and there is at least -- there is at least one example whereby the civilian police in Knin refers to the fact that they have received an order from General Cermak and takes measures in order to implement that order, and I believe that is P510.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will look at that, don't worry. First -- secondly, the fact that the order is drafted in this way could indicate no knowledge of the correct system of issuing orders to the military police. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I -- I see no -- no reason to come to such an opinion on -- on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you compare it with the other military police orders that we have seen, we have seen many, how they are set out and structured, they exist in an entirely different structure. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- is not my impression, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the orders issued by General Cermak may well look less formal or less structured than some of the other orders we have seen, be it military police or Split Military District, but as you know from D32, the 1992 service regulations, there are specific requirements to an order - it has to be clear, it has to be short, and it has to indicate who is to implement the order - and I can see these elements in the document that we see in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Next, do you know if the military police received this order?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if the Knin police station received this order?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know, because I didn't have those documents. But -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Say anything you -- feel free to say anything you want about it.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would actually be useful, then, to check, for example, UNCRO documentation to see whether the order issued by General Cermak had any effect. But I have not systematically -- I have not analysed UNCRO documentation that would address the matter, i.e., the inspection of UNCRO helicopters before each flight. As I mentioned P510 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can come to that in time. That's your one order, I know. All right. It's your one order. It is. You know. Can you say whether, if they did receive this, the military police, or the civil police viewed it as an order and followed it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean for this specific document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're going through every single order, and ...

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I cannot confirm that the military police or the civilian police received it, I can obviously not draw any conclusions as to whether they act the upon the order or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If they did receive it, do you know whether they viewed it as an order or as information?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, D32 is -- is very specific when it comes to the definition of an order and what the superior who issues the order is required to do, i.e., not only issuing it but also verify its implementation; and on the other hand, the subordinate who receives the order is also obliged to do certain things in relation to an order. The obligation to implement decisions is one of the two principles of command and control defined in Croatian armed forces doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: These are not subordinates, are they?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not subordinates in the sense of being permanently subordinated, and I'm limiting myself now to this document to draw that conclusion. However, the fact that a Colonel General with his rank and his experience uses the formulation, I order, when he wants the military police and the civilian police to do something, should mean something for those who receive the document, i.e., who receive the order. I have seen no reason, when reviewing the documents, to believe that General Cermak was unaware of which formulation he had to use, in order to have various structures in Knin do things he wanted them to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the next point is, it could be wrong to have described it as an order.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the service regulations, D32, if I remember well, specify the terminology that is to be used in an order, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, may I ask you, the question clearly invites you to admit or not to admit that it could be a mistake. Now, reference to regulations, what is there, doesn't answer the question, because you can make a mistake anyhow whatever the regulations are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. I apologise, Your Honours. I have no reason to believe that it's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you have no reason to believe it's not a mistake.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit P53, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I answer your last question or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there's no need to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that of the nine orders, 90 per cent of them concern UNCRO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You speak about nine orders. Do you refer to orders referred to in my report or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of the orders to the Knin military police and the MUP, there are nine orders, of which 90 per cent concern UNCRO.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may be possible. I haven't calculated these kind of statistics. But as pointed out at earlier occasions, it is not of quantity but also of quality, i.e., nature of the orders. And, for example, orders included in my report -- to the military police by General Cermak also refer to freedom of movement for civilians in Knin. This was also sent to the civilian police, which, in my view, is a very important order --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will be looking -- we're looking at every single one, Mr. Theunens, one by one, to see what you based your conclusion upon. So P53, this is the freedom of movement order, so-called, that goes to Knin military police, the MUP, and it concerns UNCRO. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Same questions: Do you know if the military police received this?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say whether they received this specific order but I have included --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a simple question because -- do you know whether they received it. It's just to Knin military police. It doesn't say which company, it doesn't say 72nd, it doesn't say the 7th Company, it doesn't say the Independent Company or the Joint Company. It's just as is. And you're used to analysing documents, aren't you? That's what you've told us you do?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if they received it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of the ways to determine whether they received it is to see whether any activity was undertaken by the military police following this order. And when I look at correspondence by General Forand, Sector South commander, to General Cermak, that is, for example, on English page 255, part 2 of the report, I can see -- we can see that freedom of movement by UNCRO -- for UNCRO, is a problem. General Forand believes that it's -- General Cermak is responsible for the -- what he calls unilateral restriction of movement. And we can see from 65 ter 3531, for example, mentioned on page 256, that General Cermak replies to General Forand's complaint. I agree with you that what I just said does not explicitly indicate whether the military police, yes or no, received the specific document you showed, but at least we can see that the situation that is existing corresponds with what is ordered by General Cermak to the military police in this specific document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is not the only issue concerning freedom of movement. Shouldn't you have pointed out to us that, from the 4th of August, the military police and MUP have been ordered to set up check-points? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is your question that this is not the only issue concerning freedom of movement for UNCRO or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. There are check-points set up throughout the region.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have seen -- I would -- I would hazard a guess, 20 or 30 orders from the MUP and VP dealing with check-points in the area.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is probably the case. But to my recollection, these check-points do not always apply to UNCRO. And the fact, what I just pointed out, 65 ter 2735, that General Cermak replies to a complaint by General Forand in relation to UNCRO freedom of movement shows that the issue of freedom of movement of UNCRO -- at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's the 30th of August, isn't it? Let's get the date because all this is avoided later on.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you're going to make the point --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the 11th of August for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But what I tried to say was that the fact that General Cermak reacts to a complaint by General Forand indicates that at least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to get matters -- I see on your page 255, I see a 11 of August document, UNCIVPOL chief of Sector South sends a letter to Cermak and the notification by Forand is on the 30th of August. Cermak replied on the same date. If we're talking about different dates for the same document, I might get confused in what document we're talking about. So I'd rather have this clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was unsure which is why I wanted the date because there are different dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's take the 11th of August as the date that you have cited. We've got your position on this but what it comes down to, you don't know whether the military police or the MUP, in fact, acted on this order or whether they didn't receive it or they disregarded it, do you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to summarize my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, can you answer the question? It's the question I would like answered.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This specific document does not allow to draw such a conclusion. However, when taken in context, and that is actually what analysis is about, we can see that General Cermak reacts to letters from, for example -- from UNCRO, General Forand, when the latter complains about lack of freedom of movement for UNCRO. And, for example, 65 ter 536 is a letter from General Cermak to General Forand on the 11th of August, indicating that the freedom of movement for UN members is re-established on the 11th of August, 1995, at 12.00, in order to supply themselves with food, drinks, and fuel. This is on English page 255, which means that General Cermak is in a position to influence the freedom of movement of UNCRO in a particular part of Sector South, and that he also engages in -- in -- in exchanges of -- of communications with the UNCRO commander when the latter has complaints about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us go to the next document, D788. It's the third one on the 8th of August. It's -- concerns an order, again involving UNCRO, control all entrances to the UNCRO barracks, including the main gate, particularly checks are required when refugees leave the barracks. Do not allow them to leave without adequate authorisation. Again, you don't know if the military police received this order, do you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But, I mean, I can also add that if a commander issues an order, he will verify whether it's implemented or not. One aspect of the verification of the implementation is to see whether the addressee has received it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I suppose have you to know what you're doing to know that regulation, do you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you use "you," you refer to General Cermak or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but a Colonel General, which is I believe is the most senior officer's rank in the HV, and somebody with General Cermak's experience and background, I would expect him to believe -- to know what he is doing when he is issuing order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What experience?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've just looked at his appointments.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would expect that -- that he didn't receive the rank of Colonel General as a kind of -- of -- of honorific title. I believe he was a member of the JNA -- was an officer in the JNA prior to the Croatian independence, but I'm not sure of that so I may well be wrong there, but the most important is that he has a senior rank and he uses that rank when is he the commander of the Knin garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know of other -- for instance, Mr. Sarinic, who was the advisor to President Tudjman. Do you know that he was a general as well, without having been in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Did you know in fact that there were many people in public life at that time who were given ranks, who had not been through the ranks, to achieve Colonel General in the -- by experience of the armed forces. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just checking whether I have ... Well, there are examples that people jumped ranks. Now, whether that necessarily means that these people are not able to carry out the duties that one would expect somebody with the rank they have received to carry out, is another question. I can only look at the documents that I reviewed in the framework of the preparation of the report and I see that Mr. Cermak always uses his rank of Colonel General when he is signing orders or other documents as the commander of the Knin garrison, and, as I said, there must be reasons for him to have that rank and to use the rank, including awareness of the obligations related to that rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how long, in your army, that your from, Belgium, would it take to you get to the equivalent rank of Colonel General? You were a senior captain for how long, after how many years?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rank of senior captain does not exist in the Belgian military. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were a captain?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I was a commandant. I don't recall exactly how many years it is took, but it -- approximately 12 or 13 years after finishing or graduating from Military Academy. For a Colonel General, so a three-star General, it would be a career of approximately 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we look to see, because you said the best way of looking at these things is to see what the effect was, there's an exhibit, Exhibit D147, which has been in evidence, showing the gateway to the camp on the 9th of August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If Exhibit D147 could be played, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if you could look at the film, Mr. Theunens, and what your task will be -- I won't say it's an order, a request, will be to see if there's an a military policeman, one, two, three, four, five, whatever, at the gate to the -- main gate to the UNCRO barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could play the film, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] "Reporter: Mrs. Mladenka Skaric is the first of the 840 Knin civilians who took refuge five days ago in the UNCRO barracks to return home today. When we wished her all the best in her freedom and the freedom of Croatian Knin, she told us about Milan Martic's last moments in Knin. "Mladenka Skaric: When I went down to the cellar I find President Martic down there, who was naked from waist up and barefoot, in his pants. And when I saw him I said, Mr. President, all the newspapers in the world should write about a president sharing the fate of his people in a cellar. At 7.15, he left us. "Reporter: And while you are watching as cards for returning home are filled for a large number of Knin residents who will remain in Knin, let us say that this is the result of an arrangement made today between Dr. Goran Dodig, General Ivan Cermak and Petar Pasic, government's commissioner for Knin. "Goran Dodig: I have seen General Cermak for the first time today. The way in which he is trying to resolve this, his goodwill and concrete steps with which he really wants to resolve the destiny of these people in the best possible way, fascinated me. "And this is a guarantee, along with the principled stands of the Croatian government, Croatian leadership, and President Tudjman, that everybody has a right to a free choice and that those who will remain here will have all citizenship rights. "And I think that this on the spot conduct like General Cermak's, I think this is the best guarantee that the situation will be resolved very soon to mutual satisfaction. "Ivan Cermak: They will be granted as of tomorrow full protection and all civil rights in Knin, a soup kitchen will be introduced for them. We have to urgently, with the help of civilian authorities, which, there you are, have also from today started functioning in Knin. We as a military structure in all this are helping so it goes as fast as possible. "Reporter: For the very end, a statement from Glisa Kablar of Knin and, as he himself says, a citizen of Croatia of Serb nationality. "Glisa Kablar: I intend to stay here because this is my homeland and this is, from the liberation, my state as well. Therefore, I don't plan going anywhere else but living here and staying here. And with these people, regardless how they came to argue and clash, regardless of all that, I'm staying here. To live and to work."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If that could be stopped now, that's the full clip of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We were looking at there a meeting between General Cermak and the displaced person inside the camp, essentially. We see there a view of the gates and we saw the lady going through. And would you agree, we didn't see any Croatian military police controlling the main gate to the UNCRO barracks?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the images that were shown, that is probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we particularly didn't see that lady being checked when she left the barracks?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And we can only speculate as maybe that was an accurate reflection of the situation or maybe there was an arrangement made, special arrangements were made in order to film this Croatian news feature. But I agree with you that the video as such, indeed, indicates that the lady could move freely without being checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you often speculate like that, that there had a been a special arrangement? Is that part of your methodology?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not part of my methodology to speculate, but it's part of my methodology to verify the reliability of the source and the credibility of the information, and without wanting to make general statements, because that would be contrary to the methodology, it is not unusual for parties in an armed conflict to use the media for other purposes than purely the accurate reflection -- I apologise, accurate transmission or accurate information of the events. That used to be called propaganda; now it is called in a more fashionable way, information operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you said, Do you often speculate that may be an accurate reflection. What the witness said, and we have to fairly try to understand what he means, that whether this accurately reflected the situation or whether there was an arrangement, that would be pure speculation. It is not a speculation that there was an arrangement. So, therefore, I think your question was unfair to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, and it was a point I was just taking against him, and I was -- I would have been better off moving on, rather than dealing with it. Exhibit D303, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is dated the 9th of August, 1995. It again concerns UNCRO. And it is an order to the Knin military police and Knin police station to deal with setting up a team with the task of finding UNCRO vehicles, which we know from the story of the case, had been stolen. Again, would you agree, you don't know if the commander of the Knin military police viewed this as an order or whether it was information to him about a crime that had been committed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would give the same answer as I have given before; that is, that the word "order" has, according to the regulations, particular implementations. How the military police reacted to this, we don't know. We know from another document that an order given by General Cermak is indeed acted upon by the military police and the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, did you listen to the testimony of the witness Dzolic who was the commander of the Knin military police at that time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did. I have no clear recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You didn't review what he said about this matter?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, were you aware of the fact that General Cermak needed assistance, in relation to the order that we're looking at, putting it into effect, and having it distributed around the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that the order to find these vehicles is also distributed within the Split Military District, and I believe that happened at a very late stage, that there is an order from General Gotovina to General Krsticevic, commander of the 4th Guards Brigade, in order to return UNPF vehicles who have been repainted allegedly by members of the 4th Guards Brigade. I'm just not sure whether we're talking about the same vehicles here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're going to be looking at this as a distinct matter as it's already been introduced into evidence and it tells the history of Mr. Cermak trying to deal with the matter, and it's been put forward by the Defence as demonstrating a lack of authority, so contrary to your propositions.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to add that if these are indeed the same vehicles as those General Gotovina talks about in his order to General Krsticevic, it makes sense for General Cermak to forward the order to General Gotovina because General Cermak has no authority as a garrison commander in the city of Split, which is the garrison city of the 4th Guards Brigade. It is correct that elements of the 4th Guards Brigade are in Knin at the time of the events, but I just want to highlight that the matter is more complicated than it seems by just looking at one isolated document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I am looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, that would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will have a break, and we resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Kay, there are a lot of documents in the air. I've seen that you have followed the guidance to put four documents as bar table documents. Part of the guidance was that the way in which they are described and the way in which our specific attention is drawn to certain aspects is disclosed to the other party. And, Mr. Waespi, have you read the short descriptions and comments and do you have any objections against introducing them in this way?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I might have missed that. I will go over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about that document -- if you would inform us, you don't have to respond right away. Take your time to look at it and see whether there is any objection so that we could proceed at a later stage and then assign numbers to them and decide upon admission. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Exhibit D503, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This again concerns UNCRO, Mr. Theunens. It's dated the 12th of August, 1995. It is other UNCRO equipment and vehicles that General Forand had asked General Cermak to help get returned, as they had been stolen. Order is issued, and again it goes to Knin military police, Knin police station. I don't want it repeat the same questions that we've repeated before, but the significance again that this is yet another of those orders that you're relying upon which is not part of the general nature of business in Knin relating to the military police or the civil police doing their tasks and duties. This is UNCRO specific. And doesn't that make it highly distinctive into why General Cermak issued these orders to try and help UNCRO?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that we're talking about UNCRO vehicles. But when we look at the introduction of the order, we see that the order discusses the unauthorised taking by members of the HV of these UNCRO vehicles or engineering equipment, and this brings us in the area of the maintaining of order and discipline and the duties of the garrison commander in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As we know, though, under Regulation 2 that we looked at yesterday, in fact, General Cermak cannot issue orders to HV units, only precisely prescribed regulations. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Article 54 of the 1992 service regulations, which is known here as D32, it is stated when the duties and the role of the garrison commander are discussed, that he can use the military police in order to maintain or restore order and discipline. He can also use the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you read -- sorry -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Article 54 should be read out exactly, please, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Kay, I observe that, not for the first time, that the questions and answers develop by virtue of malcommunication. I give you an example of what happened before the break. Before the break, Mr. Theunens referred to experience, and I would say rightly, Mr. Kay, you said what experience? This developed a long answer and question about how long it takes you in the Belgian army to get somewhere, whereas the issue clearly was what do we know about the experience of Mr. Cermak in the army. Instead of that, it goes in all directions and we are moving away from what the real issue was, at least that's how I understood it, that you wanted to challenge the answer that there was any such experience, which might have assisted Mr. Cermak in understanding what he was doing, as the witness told us. Now, it took us approximately one, one and a half or two pages to get to where we were. Meanwhile, I learned a lot about what positions there are in the Belgian army, what positions there are not, how much how much time it does take or does not take to reach, whereas the issue clearly was limited to the witness relying on experience, where you wanted to challenge that; and therefore, it was on my lips at that time, what do we know exactly about the time Mr. Cermak spent in military positions because we now have looked at the background but mainly about ministerial functions. Now here more or less the same happens. The question clearly focuses, Mr. Theunens, on whether this is not another example of Mr. Cermak being involved in matters in which UNCRO primarily is involved, and either you don't understand the question, or for whatever reason, you start telling us that the kind of activity develops is not foreign to a task in relation to, for example, order. Now, I understood the question to be whether this is not a very special area in which, right or wrong, orders or no orders, but it is always UNCRO that appears in these orders. That, as far as I understood, Mr. Kay, was your question. What we're doing now, we're moving away from what the real question was, and we are now somewhere in Regulation 2, Article so and so, which, at least as far as I understood the question, was not the issue you wanted to raise. And, Mr. Theunens, I would like to invite you to -- I hardly dare to say, but to analyse the question and try to understand what Mr. Kay wants to know before you answer it. And, Mr. Kay, I would invite you to not being led the witness to areas where, as far as I understand, you're not primarily interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, I wasn't interesting in going there, but the witness wanted an argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, but we went there. That's why I took a bit more time to explain what happened before the break once which took us two pages and what I felt, at this moment, felt was happening again because that takes an awful lot of time. And it's a clear example of malcommunication, I would say, in you, in understanding the question, and for Mr. Kay in giving a follow-up on matters he apparently is not that much interested in, at the moment, to hear your testimony about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, there it is, and the Court knows what the issue is. Let us just go now to P509 which is a non-UNCRO order. And remember I was telling you about the number of UNCRO orders as against other matters. This concerns an order issued by General Cermak, the 15th of August, concerning civilians and entering the town. Do you know if, in fact, the police, civil police, were in fact using their own view of the law as to whether they admitted people to the area or not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with a document, D494, where the civilian police, Split-Dalmatia police administration, submits a copy of the pass for entering the Knin garrison that had been introduced by General Cermak -- actually, the document is dated also the 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And requests the Ministry of Interior for guidance. So now, what the guidance or the decision or the reaction of the Ministry of Interior is to this request, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, if we go to D501, which is another matter but it's called a decision, and it concerns the Hotel Spas. I think it is a document that is in your report.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on English page 250, in the second part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's right. And this is a decision rather than an order. Can you explain to me the difference?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. I have not seen in the doctrine any specific definition for what is here described as a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to D504. This is it dated 11th of October, 1995. It is an order. It goes to the Knin police as well as the commission of the government of the Republic of Croatia for Knin municipality, and it concerns MUP officers being temporarily transferred to the old grammar school in Knin. Not an UNCRO order but just an order there. Are there any other orders that are to be found besides this collection that we have been through from the 8th of August and the 11th of October on this matter?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "this matter," could you please specify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Orders that you cite as being orders to the military police or civil police that are relied upon by you for your proposition concerning Mr. Cermak being superior and running the military police or the civil police. I've got them in my hand here. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look in my report. I think you provided a good summary. There are some references in other documents, for example, P1147, where General Cermak informs the addressee of his letter that he has ordered the military police to conduct an investigation, for example, but, otherwise, this corresponds with the majority of the documents that can be found in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is it, from everything that we have looked at. Is that right? I'm not concerned to what he says in letters or anything like that but actual orders that provide the foundation for your proposition.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether we saw P510?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could Exhibit P510 come up on the screen, please, under seal. Sorry, that's -- P510 is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore not to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you will -- it depends on what questions you'll put to the question whether we have to go into private session. If you just ask him whether he has seen the document then, of course, there is no need. But I think I would not be surprised if your first question would be whether this was an order issued by Mr. Cermak, P510.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness mentioned it as being one that he'd missed. Now I know why it's being dealt with separately in my file, which is my inadvertence. We have P510, we can just have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's not, in fact, an order as such but referring to the document that we have already seen concerning P509. It is linked to it and the Court has heard evidence about this. It's not a separate order. It's linked.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. But it is an example of an order by General Cermak to the civilian police being reacted upon by the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is there any such other document as this?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the material I was able to review.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That matter can now be taken off the screen as we have finished it. The Court will recollect the evidence concerning this particular matter. And the next matter we will be looking at will be, in fact, the issue of the passes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is it correct, rather than me having to produce a whole series of documents, that there are in fact a number of orders issued by the Ministry of Defence and the military [sic] of police administration from the 3rd of August onwards, concerning check-points and the establishment of those check-points by the military police and the civil police, as part of their duties?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm not sure whether the two matters are connected, and if they are connected, in which manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can we look now at a document concerning 2D07-0390, which comes from the political administration information staff in Zagreb, dated the 7th of August, and sent to the Ministry of Interior, concerning a large number of international journalists and giving their consent, in relation to these journalists being able to move in the area. Is this a document you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Would you agree that it was not exclusively Mr. Cermak who dealt with the issue concerning freedom of movement but that other agencies did as well?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it covers different aspects of freedom of movement; UNCRO, international media, local population, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at 2D --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May that document be made an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D1012, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1012 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May we look at 2D07-0228.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 5th of August, 1995. It's from the Split-Dalmatia police, issued by Mr. Cipci. If you'll remember, it's Mr. Cipci who writes on those letters concerning the validity of the passes that Mr. Cermak had signed and which were being queried by the MUP. Do you remember that, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that was D494.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Here, Mr. Cipci is giving a passage in relation to a journalist coming to a check-point in the direction of Knin and that Major Tolj had enabled him to have unobstructed arrival to Knin. A document you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But it -- I mean, it looks like a usual document that one tries to control the -- the freedom of movement of -- of journalists in an area where military operations are conducted, for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to another document, 2D07-0232.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's again from Mr. Cipci, dated the 8th of August, and asks for an opinion, because there is a great pressure to visit the liberated areas of Vrlika, Knin, Drnis by refugees, citizens, various associations, political parties, other institutions. So he was sending this letter to the operative headquarters of the MUP for their opinion as to who to give passes to. Did you appreciate that it was not only passes stamped by Mr. Cermak that were being issued to give freedom of movement to people in the area?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be admitted into evidence, Your Honour, as well as the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections to both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document ID 2D07-0228 becomes Exhibit number D1013. Document ID number 2D07-0232 becomes Exhibit number D1014.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1013 and D1014 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a whole series of documents following this same theme, and to save Court time and having dealt with it in a brief form, we will be putting them in bar table form, subject to the Court's approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then under the similar guidance --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as before, so, for example, we now have a journalist, what I would expect in the comment is the same but now about -- what is it -- various associations, political parties, et cetera, where the earlier was about journalists. If it could be introduced in this way, then our attention is drawn to relevant aspects and also relevant differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: These passes were not only being issued to journalists but also to employees of banks. Were you aware of that? Exhibit D488 is also a document concerning people from the Split Bank Limited. Were you aware of that, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the specific example but, again, it makes sense that the authority who has the power to do so controls the access of people who are not directly involved in military operations to the zone of operations. And I mean by control, not just verifying but also preventing those who should not be entitled to enter, to prevent them from entering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to this matter, did you appreciate that there was a problem, and we could see part of it within the video-clip that we saw about an hour ago, concerning the identification cards, that those citizens had under the previous Yugoslavia government who did not have Republic of Croatia identifications when the territory was liberated on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that people living in the -- in the so-called RSK did not have Croatian documents, but I have difficulties to connect it to the video images we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There was an old lady who had an ID card put on the table and we saw a picture of a propusnice, a document that you have referred to in your report, which is the document to enable people to have freedom of passage which was signed by Mr. Cermak. Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you know that General Forand had a meeting on the 8th of August with General Gotovina concerning freedom of movement and that he was told that maps would be provided showing areas in which it was safe to travel?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I mean, if you refresh my memory with a document, then I can provide more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's P359, and it is at page 3 of that document, and it's an UNCRO sitrep report signed by General Forand. Did you know that the map that was attached to Mr. Cermak's letter, Exhibit P405, when he wrote to General Forand about the freedom of movement in the area at that time, was that map? Were you aware of that fact when you were writing your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure whether I used any of these documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- 405 or P359 in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, you don't. And I don't know whether that is because you don't know of them or whether you chose not to.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you show me the documents then that could refresh my memory in order to see whether I have seen them before --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P405 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's the document there. And do you see the enclosure of the map?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. And I believe that I have included that document in my report, I mean, the advice to only use the main roads. I'm just trying to locate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The issue is the map. Did you appreciate that the map was something that General Forand had been told he would be supplied, showing him the areas that are safe to travel, when he had met General Gotovina on the 8th of August, before he met General Cermak? Did you appreciate that fact?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen the map attached to P405.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the fact rather than the map. It's the issue of why General Cermak has a letter with the map.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the question is whether the map is the same map that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you appreciated this when you wrote your report, that the -- about this matter concerning freedom of movement? It's a matter -- the freedom of movement, General Cermak's role in the matter is something that you stress in your report on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. Could you please repeat the question because it is not clear to me what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you appreciated that the map enclosed with General Cermak's letter, Exhibit P405, had earlier been referred to by General Gotovina to General Forand, at a meeting of the two men, before General Forand met General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be helpful to me to see P395 because --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll read the relevant portion of it for you. The relevant portion is: "General Gotovina spent some time talking about freedom of movement. He did not ask commander Sector South opinion. He stated that he must limit our freedom of movement out concerned for our safety. He said that maps would be provided, showing the area that is safe to travel." I read it, Mr. Kay, also because you're talking about the map whereas in this sitrep the plural is used, maps. That was what Mr. Kay was referring to, if I'm not mistaken, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen the map or maps, but I know from a statement from General Cermak that he states that he and General Gotovina are in constant coordination. So if the same maps are being used by both Generals, it could be an indication of the degree of coordination between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That document is dated the 21st of August and not on this issue. Isn't that right, where your quote comes from?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me, but I'm not sure whether the document that according to you is dated 21st of August explains or establishes when the coordination has started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're -- we're suffering now from the same problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question simply was whether you had appreciated that the map enclosed with General Cermak's letter had earlier been referred to by General Gotovina to General Forand at a meeting of the two men before General Forand met General Cermak. That was the question. Now that questions consists of two elements. First, were you aware that, in a meeting, that it was reported that in a meeting between General Gotovina and General Forand that General Gotovina said, We'll provide you with maps, safe areas. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then may I take it that you also could not tell us anything about whether the maps General Gotovina is talking about would be the same or that the map attached to the letter would be among the same maps as General Gotovina was talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. And that was the start of -- of also my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it developed in a way which seems to be a bit symptomatic for what, now and then, happens in this courtroom. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware that those propusnices were also issued by Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Should we look at Exhibit D489? There is a document dated the 9th of August, certificate of confirmation, confirming that Mr. Pasic, head of office for refugees of the municipality of Knin, took up the passes for entering into Knin garrison from 51 to 250, and he commits to deliver verified signatures of people to whom passes were given by the 10th of August, 1995. Were you aware of a large number of passes being issued by Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this document before, so I'm not aware of that but it -- based -- I mean, what I see in this document that is actually that Pasic does it under the -- or with the authorisation of General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The documents are signed by him but who receives them, who gets them is by Mr. Pasic. The Court has seen Exhibits D491 to 493 previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document I would like to look at is Exhibit D300.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit D300 is dated the 9th of August and is signed by General Cermak as information concerning various rights of people. And it is put this way: "We hereby inform all the population of Knin that has fled that the following is guaranteed to them ..." This is a document cited by you in your report at page 15 in the executive summary. You characterize it this way: "Cermak, on the 9th of August, 1995, advises all people who left Knin in 1991 to 1992 conflict of their rights." Would you agree that that is in fact incorrect, that General Cermak gave this information to all the population of Knin --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct on the face of the document, but my interpretation of the document in context of all the other documents is that it referred to the people who had -- or who fled Knin between 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate in that video-clip we saw earlier this afternoon that Mr. Cermak was, in fact, referring to those rights to those people in front of him who were the Committee of Displaced Persons that he met that afternoon, on the 9th of August, at the UNCRO camp where that film was taken?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I mean, I didn't have the video or I didn't review the video at the time of the drafting of my report. But from the images I saw, it appears that indeed that's what the images show.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you agree that this is a matter to which you could have come to an incorrect conclusion upon from your analysis?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course if you would show me additional information or other documents that would be more specific, then I would review them and obviously, if necessary, amend or change the conclusion. But I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've heard evidence about this, by the way, in the trial.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I compared, on one hand, this information; and, on the other hand, the situation of the people who were staying at the UNCRO barracks in Knin. And comparing these two different aspects led me to conclude that the information, which is D300, applies to people who fled Knin between -- I mean, due to the 1991/1992 conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why would those people at point 7 need movement permits if they already had Croatian identity cards?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what is meant by the movement permits, but indeed, it is a genuine point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Why would they need the listing of all deceased and their burial in cemeteries according to place of residence?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my view, it is information that is needed in order to establish who is entitled to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm going to leave this matter with the Trial Chamber, of course, and not go further into it in the interests of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could we turn to D495, please. Exhibit D495 comes in reverse order, if you like. The attachment comes first and then the letter second. So can we go to page 2 of D495.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which is a letter dated 15th of August concerning the passes, signed by Mr. Cipci, and asking about the validity of these passes for civilian persons in question. Is this a document you've seen before?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I was under the understanding that it was D494, so I may have made an error. Or maybe D494 is a similar document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we go to the first page now of Exhibit D495.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We see the handwritten down at the bottom, and the history of this document is known through other evidence to the Trial Chamber, that it's written here: "According to the MUP staff announcement, Colonel General Cermak's permit is valid only for military personnel and civilians working in the Croatian army." And then: "I will inform the staff of the MUP that all passes be revoked until further notice, along with the checking of all people who are travelling on roads and rails." Were you aware of this handwritten information on this document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you appreciate that in the significance -- the significance of the document, in relation to the information and propositions in your report concerning the authority of General Cermak and the significance of the passes?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there appears to be a contradiction between, on one hand, the information issued by General Cermak on the 9th, and, on the other hand, these passes. But I would still expect that somebody with the experience and background of General Cermak and holding the position he holds, that he was well aware of what he was doing when he issued the information on the 9th of August. As to how this was to be implemented, obviously there would be a requirement for coordination and cooperation with the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you appreciate that in the circumstances in Knin from the 5th of August, 1995, and onwards, for the rest of August, that there was a great deal of confusion between all the agencies of the government as to who had what responsibility and that the agencies were not synchronized in the way that you would expect, as you have just answered, concerning coordination?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that at least in the beginning, and we see that -- we have also seen that while discussing the military documents, that there are certain difficulties, especially in the manner or in the approach towards the crimes that are developing or that are being committed, i.e., the burning and the looting. However, you have shown a number of documents, including this document, that indicate that already at an early stage, for example, the Ministry of Interior or the local police through the Ministry of Interior, is looking for ways in order to come to a more coherent approach, and I would -- again, I have no document to prove that, but I would assume that General Cermak, being the commander of the Knin garrison, would be involved in that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking further at the tasks now of General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we go to Exhibit P463, to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is another presidential transcript of the 22nd of August, 1995. It is a meeting between Dr. Jure Radic, President Tudjman, and records a discussion between the two men. At one passage, there is discussion concerning General Cermak. First of all, have you seen this transcript?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us look at this conversation with Dr. Radic in the middle of the page, where he refers to: "The civil is in but according to my estimate the main problem here is the army/police relationship, because there is nothing the police can do to the army. If someone shows up as the army, then problems will come right after that. We have to have the civil authorities in the villages. Cermak is not holding power in Knin, he's not the one who can say who's going to enter which house, who is doing what. That is just an example I'm telling you." "President: Wait a second, hadn't I sent Cermak to Knin, it would have been horrible there." And Dr. Radic agrees, saying maybe he didn't use the right example precisely because we are all using it ... military authority cannot run civil matters in the terrain, military authority cannot decide on who goes to which house. "It cannot," says the president, "but it can maintain order in these transitional periods." You have relied upon the presidential transcript in the preparation of your report that we have previously referred to concerning order and the description by Mr. Cermak of his job in his discussion in 1999 with the president. In relation to your report, is there any reason why you did not seek further presidential transcripts to find out what was being said about General Cermak's job by the president?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not systematically reviewed all the presidential transcripts. I reviewed those that appeared during my searches. Now, in the context of the powers of General Cermak in Knin, I have not seen a document by General Cermak in which he complains that he is not in a position to exercise or does not have the powers to exercise the authority that has been given to him by President Tudjman. So I do appreciate what is -- what is written here, and it's an opinion by Mr. Radic about what appears to be the difficulties Mr. Cermak is facing in Knin, but as I said, I have not seen such a document authored by Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can finish this subject with one last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because otherwise we'll end up after 7.00. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For your methodology and your work, don't you think it important for you to analyse such contemporaneous statements by people at the time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you that this is an important document which, if I had seen it, I would certainly have included it in my analysis. But again, when compared with the other material I reviewed, it does not lead me to review the conclusions I drew in relation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that is apparently not what Mr. Kay is asking you. Mr. Kay is not asking you whether if you would have known this, you would have drawn different conclusions. He is mainly focussing on the importance of this document to be considered when writing a report. And this brings me, Mr. Kay --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's -- Your Honour, there is another page of this document but it will go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's -- if --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- further and I can stop here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it brings me back again, Mr. Theunens, to what I said earlier to you, is try to -- you're an analyst. Try to analyse what is exactly asked, try to understand what is asked of you. And also when you said -- when you said you didn't know whether these were the same maps, you told me that this was the start also of your previous answer. It was not. Your previous answer started by saying, I have not seen the maps; whereas, the question was whether you were aware of in a meeting between General Gotovina and General Forand, that a map was announced. That was asked. And then Mr. Kay suggested that that might have been the same map. Now, just by saying, I haven't seen the maps, I know a lot of things without sometimes having seen -- for example, I knew that reference was made to that map, even without ever having seen that map. So, therefore, it seems that you, more or less, responded also to my light critical note that you should focus on the question. After you have said, I have not seen the maps, which is certainly not an answer to the question that was put to you, you immediately drifted to coordination matters which were not asked. So, therefore, perhaps you would be so kind to consider this and especially keep this in mind when you continue your testimony tomorrow. You will continue it after I have instructed you not to speak with anyone about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. We adjourn, and we resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 4th of December, at quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of December, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.
